units.unit: Researching how rent regulation affects subdivided flats in Hong Kong
Question of whether capping rents helps tenants or shrinks the market
Key thing to test is whether capping initial rents shrinks supply of subdivided flats
Wants evidence on stock or landlord behaviour under rent controls
Wants material on how tenants weigh rent against security
Core evidence on stock
Tenant preferences
Berlin case
Supply elasticity
Needs sources on how rules are actually enforced
Needs what tenants themselves say about their landlords
Needs the legal side of a cap
Start with enforcement capacity
Needs source showing how many flats inspectors can check in a year
Needs what happens to tenants with no written agreement when a cap is enforced
Enforcement capacity
Tenant accounts
Legal risk for the claims
Needs the other tenant story about landlord converting cubicles to storage and the waiting list
Needs legal point about a banded cap being defensible
Needs the NGO's own recommendation
Tenant story shows even someone who'd gain from a cap doubts landlords would stay
Tenant story works as counter-view to the idea that capping rent keeps units on the market
Legal point backs the claim that a banded cap is defensible where a hard cap isn't
NGO recommendation backs the claim that the narrow tightening is the better package
Tenant counter-view
Banded cap legality
NGO recommendation
Tenant counter-view
Banded cap legality
NGO recommendation
All are cited documents on the shortlist still wanted
Needs the government's own framing of the floor-standard and rent band package
Wants the government's own framing to weigh its stated rationale for a floor standard plus rent band against arguments for a hard cap
The framing should back up what the package actually proposes
All cited sources still needing passages on this shortlist
Still needs the internal enforcement minute and the Mrs Wong tenant interview
Enforcement minute should show what the subcommittee found about inspection capacity and which tenants get missed
That finding is the basis for saying enforcement would fail the most exploited
Mrs Wong's account should show how tenants see the cap and whether their experience matches it
Needs enforcement minute and tenant interview passages to ground those claims
Still needs the original 2021 ordinance text and the Berlin wrap-up passages
Ordinance text is to show the 2021 law only limited increases within a tenancy, not starting rents
So the stable stock doesn't tell us what a hard cap would do
Berlin wrap-up is to show suppressed increases released once the cap was struck down and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend
Needs ordinance scope, Berlin aftermath, and policy arguments already relied on
SDU stock rose from about 107,300 in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025, so the 2021 rules didn't visibly push landlords out
Academic work separates two kinds of control: caps on the rent level shrink supply, rules limiting increases within a tenancy have small or no stock effect
Modelled Hong Kong case: a 15 percent cut in starting rents helps current tenants by roughly 900 dollars a month
But leaves 3,000 to 4,000 households a year unable to get in, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households, exactly the people the policy is meant to help
A real initial-rent cap would need a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to build
Own conclusion: a light band plus real security of tenure protects the people the current market abandons without pretending the waiting list is a rent problem
The load-bearing step is the entry-loss figure
If a modest cut in starting rents didn't block new households, the case against a hard cap would weaken a lot
The stock index and the two-types distinction matter mostly as context
Would want to know the model's assumptions about how many new households try to enter each year and how sensitive entry is to rent level
If it assumes a fixed inflow and a steep response, the 3,000–4,000 could be soft
Would like to check whether the model lets landlords convert units to storage instead of just exiting
The point being made is that a hard cap helps current tenants but pushes the cost onto people trying to get in
That is why a light, indexed band on starting rents with tenure tightened first is preferred
The stock numbers and the two-kinds-of-control distinction are just context; they don't prove a binding cap would be harmless
The claim that needs backing is that the losers from a hard cap are mainly the households still outside, exactly the people the policy is meant to help
A source would need to show who actually gets shut out when a cap binds — that the households blocked from entering are new arrivals and newly formed households, rather than existing tenants.
